newsitem.title: TANZANIA: FEATURE - Tanzania's former slave port, a crumbling ruin.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Tanzania's former slave port, a crumbling ruin.

text.p: It is quiet along the Bagamoyo seafront now. The tide is out and save for a staccato burst of laughter drifting up from a gaggle of fishermen tending their laid-up dhow, there is little activity.
Overlooking the fishing enterprise stands a stout, solitary building, locally known as the old German customs house.
Emerging from its shadows, an old man called Ngangati proffers a handful of corroded, colonial-era German coins. "Business is bad -- how much will you give me for these?" he asks.
Business has not always been bad in Bagamoyo.
With trade links stretching to India and the Gulf, by the 19th century it was a flourishing centre of commerce and politics.
A common port of call on the east African coast, the town was a familiar destination on a mariner's chart.
The industry to which Bagamoyo's name is irrevocably linked is slavery.
LAST GLIMPSE OF AFRICA
The coastal town was the terminus for the vast slave and ivory caravans emerging from the African interior.
The beach, now used by local fishermen to land their catch, used to echo to the clank of hundreds of chains. Columns of slaves and their Arab captors filed out to board waiting dhows for transport.
Their destination was the slave market on Zanzibar island, 30 km (19 miles) west across a shark-infested strait.
For tens of thousands of slaves, Bagamoyo was their last glimpse of Africa.
The name Bagamoyo is said to derive from Kiswahili for "crush your heart", the name slaves gave to the caravanserai because once arrived, all hope of freedom was lost.
The town lies about 65 km (40 miles) north of Tanzania's main port city, Dar es Salaam.
At the outskirts, the bitumen ends and a bone-jolting, pot-holed track wends its way through scattered farming communities and banana and coconut plantations, lush and green after seasonal rains.
Skirting an earlier Muslim settlement at Kaole, the road spears northeast, picking up the old slave track stretching 1,200 km (745 miles) west to Ujiji and Kigoma on the shores of Lake Tanganyika.
NEGLECTED BUILDINGS TELL STORY OF SUFFERING
Today, most of Bagamoyo's historic architecture, an eclectic mix of African and Arab culture and German colonisation, is crumbling into disrepair.
A former slave prison, converted by German authorities into a fort, is still intact, along with the former administration building, its shuttered exteriors streaked with mildew.
A nearby plaque marks the spot where British explorers Richard Burton and John Hanning Speke first stepped ashore in 1859 on their quest to discover the source of the Nile.
A church, where in 1874 the embalmed body of Africa's most celebrated opponent of slavery, Dr David Livingstone, was brought, still stands, part of the historic Roman Catholic mission.
Yellowing documents inside the mission's small museum describe contemporary accounts of the horror of slavery, a trade that reached its peak in the mid-1850s but continued until 1922.
"The routes of the slave caravans were marked by the bones of thousands of dead people," said one anonymous witness.
SLAVES DIED IN THOUSANDS ON TREK TO COAST
The march from the interior to the coast could take between three to six months. On average, five died for every slave still alive by the time the caravan reached Bagamoyo.
The mission records show 10,000 slaves were registered through Bagamoyo in 1811, increasing to 50,000 in 1839 and between 50,000 and 70,000 per year from 1860-1870.

A photograph shows the "last known ex-slave of the mission," Maria Ernestina. Kidnapped from her village in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo, she was brought with her mother to Bagamoyo.

The German authorities confiscated the captives and Ernestina was ordered to serve as domestic help with a European family. She escaped and lived in the mission and later in Bagamoyo before "dying of great age" in 1974.
Local people say the government has ignored their welfare and that little financial aid is given to their historic town. They say cholera and malaria is rife in the district.
"This place is sacred to our (Tanzanian) memory. I hope the government can improve things. It's so bad. Every year, every year, they promise," said resident Saleh Deudi.
